name: Cartalax
maker: St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology (V. Khavinson)

overview.headline: A three-amino-acid peptide sold for joints. The published studies are on skin, kidney and stem cells, not cartilage.
overview.lede: Cartalax is the Khavinson institute's tripeptide Ala-Glu-Asp. Vendors sell it for cartilage and joints, yet we could not find a single published study of it in cartilage, joint tissue or people with joint disease. The papers that exist are cell-culture work on skin fibroblasts, kidney tissue and stem cells. It is not a registered medicine anywhere.

mechanism.intro: A short peptide said to slow cell ageing in connective tissue.

parts.name: The bioregulator idea
parts.text: The 2016 computer model places Cartalax on the DNA sequence "acct" with only "weak" predicted binding, three times weaker than the tetrapeptide Pancragen at the same site. A docking calculation, not a measurement in tissue.

parts.name: What the cell work showed
parts.text: Ala-Glu-Asp was tested on ageing skin fibroblasts (2016), kidney tissue cultures (2015), human mesenchymal stem cells (2020) and dental-ligament stem cells from 10 donors (2019), where significant effects were reported for a four-peptide mixture and for the tripeptide KED, not for Ala-Glu-Asp alone. No cartilage experiment appears anywhere.

more.title: More: where the name comes from
paras: Each institute extract had a synthetic peptide designed to match it. Cartalax was assigned to cartilage, but unlike Bronchogen (bronchial cells) or Livagen (liver cells) the institute never published an experiment in the named tissue.

results.headline: Skin, kidney and stem cells in a dish, old-rat kidneys, and nothing about joints or people.
results.lede: Every published Cartalax experiment is in cultured cells or rodent kidney. None measures cartilage, pain, mobility or any joint outcome.

stats.lbl: donors whose dental-ligament stem cells were tested in the 2019 Italian–Russian study, the only human-cell data

items.t: Human skin fibroblasts ageing in culture (Lin'kova 2016) and human mesenchymal stem cells (Ashapkin 2020): gene-expression changes reported by the institute. Periodontal ligament stem cells from 10 donors (Caputi 2019): a four-peptide mixture raised the nerve-growth protein GAP43; Ala-Glu-Asp alone was not reported as significant. Kidney tissue cultures (Chalisova 2015).
Old rats: kidney structure and function reported as improved with peptides including Ala-Glu-Asp (Zamorskii 2019). No cartilage or joint experiment in any species.
None found. Cartalax is absent from the institute's 2014 clinical review and from its 2020 monograph's human data.

more.title: More: why a name is not evidence
paras: A product called Cartalax, sold for joints, with no cartilage study is a marketing fact, not a scientific one. The Italian stem-cell work is a collaboration with Khavinson as co-author, not an independent test.

effects.headline: No safety data in people or animals beyond cell cultures and one rat kidney study.
effects.lede: Unlike several of its siblings, Cartalax has no U.S. patent with toxicity testing and no human report of any kind.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not measurable: no trial has been run and no human report exists.

unique.title: What is actually known
unique.text: Nothing. We found no toxicity study, no human exposure and no adverse-event report for this peptide.

more.title: More: what a trial would monitor for
paras: Joint symptoms and imaging, if the claim were tested; kidney function, the only organ it has been shown to affect in a living animal; immune reactions.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: In cultured skin, kidney and stem cells: changes in growth and gene markers. In old rats: better-looking kidneys. In joints or people: nothing measured.

urgent.title: Symptoms a doctor should see promptly
items: Spreading redness, swelling or pus at an injection site, or fever and chills after an injection
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
A hot, swollen or newly painful joint, which needs a doctor regardless of cause
urgent.note: No trial has defined this peptide's own danger signs; these relate to an unverified product.

levels.nopk: No one has measured Cartalax in a person's blood; no half-life or absorption figure exists for it in any species. There is nothing to build a curve from.

stats.lbl: toxicity or pharmacokinetic studies in any species
stats.src: PubMed, patents, institute publications and registries, Oct 2026

explain.t: The simulator on other pages needs a measured half-life; none exists for Cartalax.

explain.b: Why the oral claim is contested.
explain.t: Pharmacologists expect peptides this short to be digested by gut and blood enzymes; the institute says they are absorbed intact. Nothing in people settles it.

more.title: More: what this page cannot tell you
paras: What is in a product sold as Cartalax, or what repeated use does: no independent analysis exists, and no study has followed anyone beyond a few weeks.

trials.headline: No clinical trial, registered or unregistered, could be found.
trials.lede: Cartalax has never been given to people in any published study.

more.title: More: how the existing studies were run
paras: Cultured skin, kidney and stem cells were exposed to the peptide and compared with untreated cultures; old rats were given peptides and their kidneys examined. None of this says anything about joints, or about a person.

running.title: No registered trials
items: No clinical trial of Cartalax on ClinicalTrials.gov or any registry we could find (October 2026).
No Russian clinical report of Cartalax, controlled or uncontrolled, was found.

find.text: Search the registry for "Cartalax" and its sequence "AED". We found no registered trial.

status.headline: Not approved anywhere. Sold for joints with no joint study.

items.label: Canada
items.text: Never authorised by Health Canada as a medicine or natural health product (October 2026).

items.label: United States
items.text: Not FDA-approved; absent from FDA's 503A compounding category list of 14 May 2026.

items.label: Russia
items.text: Not a registered medicine; not among the institute's six licensed products, and no Russian registration of any kind found.

cards.title: What a "bioregulator" claim rests on
cards.text: The claim is that a peptide copied from an organ extract reaches that organ and switches on its genes. For Cartalax the support is:
items: Computer docking models, test-tube DNA work and cell cultures from one institute; no study has tracked one of these peptides into a human organ.
No cartilage or joint experiment has been published for this peptide in any species.

cards.title: What "research use only" means
cards.text: A "research use only" label is a legal device, not a safety rating. No regulator in Canada or the U.S. has checked what is in a vial sold as Cartalax, and no toxicology or purity data have been filed in the West.
items: Whether a supplement under the name Карталакс is currently registered in Russia we could not confirm.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: If any of these appear after using such a product, see a doctor and bring the product:
items: Fever, chills, or a hot, swollen injection site
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
A hot, swollen or newly painful joint
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: the Khavinson peptide family
paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946–2024) directed the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, which made animal-organ extracts from the 1970s and then designed two- to four-amino-acid peptides from each extract's amino-acid make-up, naming them after target organs. Six products became licensed medicines in the USSR or Russia: Thymalin (1982), Thymogen and Epithalamin (1990), Prostatilen (1992), Cortexin and Retinalamin (1999). The synthetic organ-named peptides sold online are not among them, and none appears in an international trial registry.
